questions.q: In which work did François Bernier articulate his critique of Mughal land ownership, and to whom was it dedicated?
questions.a: Bernier articulated his critique in *Travels in the Mughal Empire* (published 1670–71), dedicated to Louis XIV of France. A wrong answer (e.g., naming *Rihla* or *Kitab-ul-Hind*) reveals confusion between the three travellers' works — a basic identification error that undermines all subsequent analysis.

questions.q: Bernier claimed the Mughal emperor "owned all the land." How did Abu'l Fazl, Akbar's chronicler, characterize the land revenue demand, and why does that distinction matter?
questions.a: Abu'l Fazl described land revenue as "remunerations of sovereignty" — a claim by the ruler on the *produce* for protection rendered, not rent from *owned property*. Missing this distinction means accepting Bernier's European feudal lens (landlord–tenant) for a Mughal system where the state claimed a share of the harvest, not proprietary rights over the soil.

questions.q: Apply Bernier's "no private property → no investment" logic to a modern scenario: A government leases farmland to tenants on 5-year non-renewable contracts. Predict the likely effect on soil conservation and explain whether Bernier's model holds.
questions.a: Tenants would likely skip soil-conservation investments (e.g., bunding, manuring) because benefits accrue beyond the lease — Bernier's incentive argument holds *if* tenure insecurity is real. But a wrong answer that says "Bernier was right about Mughal India" ignores that Mughal *zamindars* and *khudkasht* peasants *did* have hereditary, transferable occupancy rights — the "insecurity" was Bernier's projection, not Mughal reality.

questions.q: Analyze how Bernier's binary opposition (Europe = private property/progress; India = crown ownership/despotism) served as a "warning for Europe." What specific European political fear did he mobilize?
questions.a: Bernier warned that if European kings abolished noble/private property and claimed all land (as he thought Mughal emperors did), Europe would become "kingdoms of deserts and beggars." He mobilized the *nobility's fear* of royal absolutism — using Mughal India as a cautionary tale against centralized monarchical power in France. A wrong answer that focuses only on "India was poor" misses the *polemical purpose* of his comparison.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Bernier's account is useless for reconstructing Mughal rural society because it is ideologically biased." Defend your position with two pieces of evidence from the Mughal record.
questions.a: The statement is *partly wrong*. Bias ≠ uselessness. Bernier *accurately* notes: (1) massive precious-metal inflows (corroborated by Dutch/English factory records), and (2) existence of prosperous merchant communities (e.g., *mahajans*, *nagarsheths*). Historians use these *corroborated* details while discarding his structural theory. A wrong answer that discards the whole account fails the historian's craft of "reading against the grain."

questions.q: Construct a 3-panel cartoon strip (described in words) that shows: Panel 1 — Bernier observing a Mughal village; Panel 2 — his mental translation into "crown ownership → tyranny"; Panel 3 — Montesquieu/Marx reading Bernier and building "oriental despotism"/"Asiatic mode." Caption each panel with the *intellectual operation* occurring (e.g., "selection," "projection," "theorization").
questions.a: Panel 1: Bernier sees peasants paying high revenue → Caption: *Observation (selective: notes burden, misses hereditary occupancy)*. Panel 2: Thought bubble: "No deeds, no inheritance → king owns all → no incentive to improve" → Caption: *Projection (imposing European property categories)*. Panel 3: Montesquieu writes *Spirit of Laws*; Marx drafts *Capital* → Caption: *Theorization (elevating a traveller's trope into a universal stage of history)*. A poor answer draws only literal scenes without labeling the *epistemic moves*.

What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Bernier's Critique?
questions.a: Students often believe Bernier's "crown ownership" claim is a factual description of Mughal law because he was an eyewitness who "saw it with his own eyes." In reality, Bernier *inferred* ownership from high revenue demands and the emperor's power to resume jagirs — he never cites a Mughal legal text declaring the emperor sole proprietor.
